title: The Real Reason Good Leaders Take Vacations
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece reframes vacations from a personal wellness issue into a leadership and organizational health issue. Leaders who stay perpetually connected during time off implicitly signal to their teams that stepping away is unacceptable, which the article ties directly to organizational burnout. It also argues that a leader's absence functions as a diagnostic: if the team stalls without the leader present, that reveals over-reliance on the leader and under-empowered processes. The piece closes with the image of a rubber band pulled too taut, arguing that leaders, like their teams, need real recovery time, and that modeling disconnection is itself a leadership act, not a personal indulgence.
points: Leaders who stay connected during vacation implicitly tell their teams that time off is unacceptable.
Burnout is more common in organizations where vacations are treated as optional.
A leader's absence reveals whether the team is empowered or over-reliant on the leader as a bottleneck.
Healthy teams are described as 'player led,' not 'leader driven.'
Taking real vacation is framed as being as much about the team's health as the leader's own.
quotes: Highly connected leaders become addicted to touching base and responding to messages throughout the day.
The lesson too many leaders learned during the lockdown was how working non-stop seemed so much more acceptable
Burnout is rampant in organizations where vacations are seen as optional.
Teams work best when they are player led, not leader driven.
When the rubber band gets too taut, we can either let it unwind, or we can watch it snap.
As with so many things about leadership, vacations are as much about others as they are about you.
